keyframe_review.note: 7.99 M km2 for 1822-1823: all of Brazil plus the Cisplatina (Uruguay, 922 cells). The infobox gives 8,337,218 km2 for 1889, so the area is in order (ratio 0.96 to the 1889 figure). But when independence was declared on 7 September 1822 the Portuguese garrisons still held 'key cities such as Salvador, São Luís, Belém, and Montevideo', Maranhão and Pará 'declared loyalty to Portugal', the siege of Salvador ended only on 2 July 1823 and the Royal Volunteers left Cisplatina 'at the beginning of 1824'. The shape is the claim and stays; the ledger draws these as contested (Portuguese Empire row has no Brazilian land after 1821).

7.99 M km2, identical to 1822-1823 but for a cell. The page dates the Province of Amazonas to 1850 ('officially created by Emperor Pedro II in 1850') and the Empire page lists treaties with Peru (1851) and Uruguay (1851); no page opened dates a frontier event in 1853, so the shape stands as the claim (unverified: page budget). Reopened on 2026-10-19 (Brazil-Venezuela, Brazil-Colombia, Brazil-Peru border pages, Territorial evolution of Brazil): the Venezuela line is the treaty of 5 May 1859, the Colombian lines are of 1907 and 1928, the Peruvian limit of 1909, and none of them describes a transfer in 1853, so the north-west Amazon was not a treaty frontier then. correction.text: the 1865 shape with the land under Paraguayan occupation kept as Brazil's (status only: it is hatched by the occupation events)

keyframe_review.note: 7.959 M km2 for 1865 alone (-64,000 km2): the Paraguayan invasion snapshot. 205 cells of Mato Grosso do Sul (invaded 14 December 1864), 35 of Rio Grande do Sul (São Borja 12 June 1865, Uruguaiana surrendered 18 September 1865) and slivers of Corrientes and Misiones are out of the outline. Occupied land stays the owner's, hatched in the occupier's colour, and becomes the occupier's only if annexed (master plan, rule 4); /ledger occupation_start 1864-12 and 1865-06 carry the occupation, so the 240 Brazilian cells are put back here, as the 1866 outline does. The Argentine slivers stay out.

8.023 M km2 for 1866-1867, the 1853 outline again. The Mato Grosso do Sul land stays Brazil's under Paraguayan occupation until 1868 (/ledger occupation_end 1868, Mato Grosso campaign page: 'Paraguayan withdrawal in 1868'); the Paraguayan War page says the Paraguayans 'had left once again' Miranda in September 1866 but that 'a large portion of Mato Grosso remained under Paraguayan control' after Corumbá was liberated in June 1867.

correction.text: the 1868 shape without the Paraguayan cells (Allied occupation) and without the strip north of the Apa, which Brazil gains only on 9 January 1872

keyframe_review.note: 8.468 M km2 for 1868-1869 (+444,000 km2 on 1866): 534 cells of eastern Paraguay, 1,219 of Brazil (Amazonas 616, Mato Grosso do Sul 376, Mato Grosso 189, Rondônia 26, Acre 4), 31 of Santa Cruz in Bolivia and 3 of Argentina. Two removals. (1) The Paraguayan cells are the Allied occupation ('Humaitá fell on 25 July 1868'; 'Asunción was occupied on 1 January 1869'), not Brazilian land. (2) 345 cells (87,250 km2; Mato Grosso do Sul and a few cells beyond) are Paraguay's 1822 shape inside Brazil, none in Brazil's 1866 shape; the Loizaga-Cotegipe Treaty of 9 January 1872 ('Brazil also retained the northern regions it had claimed before the war') is the first event the pages give for them, so they are subtracted here and in 1870 and change hands at /ledger 1872-01. The paraguay dossier's 1868 and 1870 corrections also lack them (they intersect with modern Paraguay), so the strip is in neither outline in 1868-1871 unless that dossier keeps it to 1872. The other Brazilian additions come from Bolivia's 1866 shape and are carried by the two Treaty of Ayacucho events (27 March 1867): 646 cells in Amazonas, Rondônia and Acre (about 163,000 km2, against the page's 102,400 km2 'further north then annexed to the Brazilian state of Amazonas') and 261 cells (about 65,000 km2) in western Mato Grosso, Mato Grosso do Sul and Santa Cruz at confidence 1; the page, reopened, describes no line. Kept as the claim.

region.text: the whole of Brazil and the Cisplatina, as claimed in 1822

ledger.note: 7 September 1822: Pedro declares Brazil independent. 'Pedro declared Brazil completely independent of Portugal on 7 September 1822'; 'On 12 October, the prince was acclaimed Pedro I, first Emperor of the newly created Empire of Brazil.' The war with the Portuguese garrisons formally began on 1 August 1822. The land is Cliopatria's 1822 outline, the claim.

region.text: Salvador, held by the Portuguese garrison until 2 July 1823

ledger.note: 1822: the Portuguese hold Salvador. The page: Portuguese garrisons held 'key cities such as Salvador, São Luís, Belém, and Montevideo' when independence was declared; Bahia 'had no consensus at first'.

region.text: Maranhão and Pará, which 'declared loyalty to Portugal' at the outset (São Luís and Belém)

ledger.note: 1822: Maranhão and Pará stay loyal to Portugal. The northern provinces of Pará and Maranhão 'declared loyalty to Portugal' at the outset.

region.text: Cisplatina, where the Portuguese regiments 'retreated to Montevideo and were besieged by Brazilians'

ledger.note: 1822: the Portuguese regiments in Montevideo. 'Portuguese regiments retreated to Montevideo and were besieged by Brazilians' (no year on the page); the Montevideo cabildo had approved incorporation as the province of Cisplatina in 1821.

region.text: Maranhão and Pará, which 'declared loyalty to Portugal' at the outset (São Luís and Belém)

ledger.note: 1823: Maranhão and Pará fall in line. John Pascoe Grenfell page: 'In August 1823, Grenfell, now a Commander in the small brig Dom Miguel sailed to Belém do Pará' and 'The Portuguese capitulated', before the five soldiers were executed on 17 October 1823 (the surrender itself has no month or day). Thomas Cochrane page: he took command on 21 March 1823 and 'bluffed the garrison into surrender' at Maranhão, undated, and the Grenfell page has him 'using a similar tactic used by Lord Cochrane at Maranhão'. The Brazilian War of Independence page ('Cochrane secured the surrender of Maranhão and Pará') gives no date. Year 1823 is the pages' (reopened 2026-10-19); the month is not given.

region.text: Salvador, held by the Portuguese garrison until 2 July 1823

ledger.note: 2 July 1823: Salvador surrenders. 'The siege of Salvador ended with the surrender of approximately 10,000 Portuguese troops on 2 July 1823.'

region.text: Cisplatina, where the Portuguese regiments 'retreated to Montevideo and were besieged by Brazilians'

ledger.note: Beginning of 1824: the Portuguese leave Montevideo. 'Military operations ended with the withdrawal of the Royal Volunteers from Cisplatina, at the beginning of 1824.' Reviewer am-08-b: confidence 2, the page gives no month ('at the beginning of 1824').

region.text: Olinda, which Paes de Andrade held in 1824

ledger.note: 2 July 1824: Pernambuco rebels proclaim the Confederation of the Equator. 'Manuel Paes de Andrade made use of the chance and announced the independence of Pernambuco'; he held Olinda while the rest of the province did not join the revolt.

region.text: Olinda, which Paes de Andrade held in 1824

ledger.note: September 1824: the Confederation of the Equator is crushed. 'On September 12, the army led by Brigadier General Lima e Silva and Paes Barreto attacked Recife'; the rebels 'were completely defeated five days later in Olinda'.

region.text: Cisplatina, where the Portuguese regiments 'retreated to Montevideo and were besieged by Brazilians'

ledger.note: 19 April 1825: the Thirty-Three Orientals land. 'On 19 April 1825, a group of 33 men known as the Treinta y Tres' landed at Agraciada beach under Lavalleja; on 25 August the Florida assembly declared independence from Brazil and union with the United Provinces; Brazil declared war on 10 December 1825. The counterpart is the Orientals joined by the United Provinces.

region.text: Cisplatina, where the Portuguese regiments 'retreated to Montevideo and were besieged by Brazilians'

ledger.note: 27 August 1828: the Preliminary Peace Convention. 'The conflict continued until 27 August 1828', signed under British mediation.

region.text: Cisplatina, the land in the 1827 shape and not in the 1828 shape (Uruguay and slivers of Entre Ríos and Corrientes)

ledger.note: 27 August 1828: Cisplatina becomes independent as Uruguay. The 1828 Treaty of Montevideo 'acknowledged the independence of Cisplatina under the name Eastern Republic of Uruguay' and 'granted Brazil sovereignty over the eastern section of the former Eastern Jesuit Missions'; 'In Brazil, the loss of Cisplatina added to growing discontent with Emperor Pedro I.'

region.text: the province of Grão-Pará: Belém and the interior where the rebels resisted

ledger.note: 6-7 January 1835: the Cabanagem rebels take Belém. 'On the night of January 6, 1835, the rebels attacked and conquered the city of Belém'; they freed Clemente Malcher on the 7th and made him provincial president. The rebels lost and retook the capital (14 August 1835) and left it in April 1836; 'For three years, the rebels continued to resist from the interior of the province.'

region.text: Rio Grande do Sul

ledger.note: 20 September 1835: the Ragamuffin revolt begins. 'It began on 20 September 1835, when rebel forces seized Porto Alegre'; the empire recaptured the city in June 1836.

region.text: Rio Grande do Sul (and slivers of Santa Catarina, Uruguay and Argentina), the land in the 1835 shape and not in the 1836 shape

ledger.note: 11 September 1836: the Riograndense Republic is proclaimed. Antônio de Souza Neto 'declared the independence of the Riograndense, or the Republic of Piratini, on 11 September 1836', after Seival; capitals shifted inland, 'such as Piratini'.

region.text: Santa Catarina, where the rebels took Laguna in 1839

ledger.note: 1839: the rebels proclaim the Juliana Republic in Santa Catarina 'following the capture of Laguna'; it 'fell back into imperial hands after four months'. The page gives no month.

region.text: Santa Catarina, where the rebels took Laguna in 1839

ledger.note: 1839: Laguna returns to the empire after four months; the Juliana Republic is gone.

region.text: the province of Grão-Pará: Belém and the interior where the rebels resisted

ledger.note: 1840: the last Cabanagem rebels yield. 'In 1840 the last rebel group, under the leadership of Gonçalo Jorge de Magalhães, yielded'; an amnesty was declared in 1839; more than 40,000 dead.

region.text: Rio Grande do Sul

ledger.note: 1 March 1845: the Treaty of Ponche Verde ends the Ragamuffin War. 'It ended on 1 March 1845 with the Treaty of Ponche Verde': full amnesty for the rebels, the empire paid the Republic's debts.

region.text: Rio Grande do Sul (and slivers of Santa Catarina, Uruguay and Argentina), the land in the 1835 shape and not in the 1836 shape

ledger.note: 1 March 1845: Rio Grande do Sul returns to the Empire. The page has the Riograndense and Juliana Republics reintegrated into the Empire as the Brazilian states of Rio Grande do Sul and Santa Catarina. Cliopatria's shape returns in 1846.

region.text: the upper Rio Negro basin and the north-west Amazon, the land in the 1853 shape and not in the 1846 shape (lon -72.2 to -65.7, lat -4.7 to 2.0; 25 cells in Colombia)

ledger.note: 1853: the north-west Amazon enters Cliopatria's outline. The Amazonas page dates the Province of Amazonas to 1850 and gives no frontier event. Pages reopened on 2026-10-19 put the treaty lines later and describe no transfer in 1853: Brazil-Venezuela border ('delimited by the Treaty of Limits and River Navigation of May 5, 1859'), Brazil-Colombia border (treaties of 1907 and 1928), Brazil-Peru border (limit 'established in the Treaty of Rio de Janeiro in 1909'; the 1851 treaty is not on the page). The 794 cells (200,803 km2) are bridged from the shape (pages silent): a claim, not a treaty line, held as a gain from nobody at confidence 1. [Fx-52 (K11): the 768 Brazilian cells of this region are now drawn as Brazilian from 1824 by the keyframes of 1824-1846 (Amazonas page: the comarca of Rio Negro 'was incorporated into the Empire of Brazil in 1824'), so this gain finds only the remaining cells, those of the Colombian side (about 25).]

region.text: the Mato Grosso districts the Paraguayans took: Albuquerque, Tage and Corumbá (January 1865), Coxim (April), then Nioaque and Miranda

ledger.note: 14 December 1864: Paraguay invades Mato Grosso and holds the southern districts (the owner's side of paraguay /ledger/4, roles reversed; hatched over Brazil's land, not contested). 'launching the Mato Grosso campaign by invading the Brazilian province of Mato Grosso on 14 December 1864'; the Mato Grosso campaign page has Corumbá taken in January 1865 and 'Coxim was taken in April 1865'. The zone is the paraguay dossier's: Paraguay's 1865 shape in Mato Grosso do Sul, 542 cells, of which 205 are Brazilian land taken in the war and 337 the disputed strip north of the Apa, which Paraguay held before the war and which changes hands at the 1872 gain below.

region.text: São Borja (12 June 1865), Itaqui and Uruguaiana (6 August)

ledger.note: 12 June 1865: the Paraguayans take São Borja and hold the Uruguay river towns (the owner's side of paraguay /ledger/6). The capture of São Borja is dated '12 June'; Uruguaiana fell on 6 August and Itaqui too. Mirrored from the paraguay dossier; 35 cells of Rio Grande do Sul.

region.text: São Borja (12 June 1865), Itaqui and Uruguaiana (6 August)

ledger.note: 18 September 1865: Uruguaiana surrenders and the occupation of Rio Grande do Sul ends (the owner's side of paraguay /ledger/7). 'On 18 September, the Paraguayan garrison surrendered without further bloodshed.'

region.text: the land 'further north then annexed to the Brazilian state of Amazonas', as far as the 1868 shape draws it (the land in the 1868 shape and not in the 1866 shape, in Amazonas, Rondônia and Acre)

ledger.note: 27 March 1867: the Treaty of Ayacucho with Bolivia. The treaty (infobox 'Signed: 27 March 1867', La Paz) 'assigned the land of Acre to Bolivia in exchange for 102,400 square kilometers of territory further north then annexed to the Brazilian state of Amazonas'. The page does not describe the line; the shape adds about 163,000 km2 in Amazonas, Rondônia and Acre in 1868. Reopened on 2026-10-19: the page names no river or line ('Demarcation of the borders was not started until the end of the 19th century') and the 646 cells are the part of the transfer inside Amazonas, Rondônia and Acre; the rest of the land Bolivia's 1866 shape loses is the next event.

region.text: the rest of the land that Bolivia's 1866 shape has and Brazil's 1868 shape draws: 228 cells in western Mato Grosso and Mato Grosso do Sul (lon -60.5 to -57.2, lat -19.9 to -14.0), 31 in Santa Cruz and 2 elsewhere

ledger.note: Bridged to the same treaty of 27 March 1867. The page names only the 102,400 km2 'further north then annexed to the Brazilian state of Amazonas' and mentions Mato Grosso only for the 1903 Treaty of Petrópolis 'concessions in the state of Mato Grosso'; it says nothing of these 261 cells (about 65,000 km2), which Bolivia's 1866 shape has and its 1868 shape does not, and Brazil's 1868 shape draws. With the previous event the whole Bolivian loss between the 1866 and 1868 shapes is accounted for; the date is the treaty's, the land is the shapes' reading (page silent).

region.text: the Mato Grosso districts the Paraguayans took: Albuquerque, Tage and Corumbá (January 1865), Coxim (April), then Nioaque and Miranda

ledger.note: 1868: Paraguay withdraws from Mato Grosso (the owner's side of paraguay /ledger/10, which is confidence 1). The Mato Grosso campaign page gives, in its infobox, 'Date: December 1864 – April 1868' and 'Result: Initial Paraguayan conquest; Paraguayan withdrawal in 1868'; its text describes no withdrawal. The Paraguayan War page's 'The Brazilians withdrew from the area in April 1868, moving their troops to the main theatre of operations' is about Brazilian troops, and after Corumbá was liberated in June 1867 'a large portion of Mato Grosso remained under Paraguayan control'. Year 1868 is the page's, the month is not given.

region.text: the Paraguayan land the Allies overran in 1868-1870, as Cliopatria's Brazil shape draws it

ledger.note: 25 July 1868: Humaitá falls and the Allies overrun Paraguay. 'Humaitá fell on 25 July 1868, after a long siege'; 'Asunción was occupied on 1 January 1869, by Brazilian general'; the Allies were in Paraguay from the crossing of the Paraná on 16 April 1866. Argentine and Brazilian troops occupied it together.

region.text: 'the northern regions it had claimed before the war' (the disputed territories north of the Apa River; same zone as the paraguay dossier)

ledger.note: 9 January 1872: the Loizaga-Cotegipe Treaty. 'Brazil signed a separate Loizaga–Cotegipe Treaty of peace and borders with Paraguay on 9 January 1872'; 'Brazil also retained the northern regions it had claimed before the war.' Mirrors the paraguay dossier's loss. The strip is 345 cells (87,250 km2) of Paraguay's 1822 shape inside modern Brazil, none of them in Brazil's 1866 shape; Cliopatria's Brazil 1868 and 1870 shapes draw it four years early, so the corrections of those keyframes subtract it and this is where it changes hands. The Paraguayan War page does not say who held it in 1868-1871 and describes no Brazilian occupation of the Apa region.

region.text: the Paraguayan land the Allies overran in 1868-1870, as Cliopatria's Brazil shape draws it

ledger.note: 1876: the Allied occupation of Paraguay ends. 'Argentine and Brazilian troops occupied Paraguay until 1876.' The page gives no month; the Machaín-Irigoyen Treaty (3 February 1876) completed the Argentine side.

region.text: the 40 cells of Roraima in the 1877 shape and not in the 1870 shape (about 10,000 km2)

ledger.note: 1877: 40 cells of Roraima enter the outline, held by no Cliopatria shape in 1870. The Brazil-Venezuela border page says the border was 'delimited by the Treaty of Limits and River Navigation of May 5, 1859' and follows the Amazon-Orinoco watershed to Mount Roraima; it dates no change in the 1870s (page silent). Dated by the shape's start year, bridged at confidence 1.

region.text: the whole Empire at its end

ledger.note: 15 November 1889: the republican coup ends the Empire. 'The coup took place on 15 November 1889', in which the rebels 'launched a coup and instituted the republic'; slavery had been abolished on 13 May 1888 (Golden Law). Area 8,337,218 km2 (infobox, 1889).

wars.name: Brazilian War of Independence

zones.text: Salvador, held by the Portuguese garrison until 2 July 1823
Maranhão and Pará, which 'declared loyalty to Portugal' at the outset (São Luís and Belém)
Cisplatina, where the Portuguese regiments 'retreated to Montevideo and were besieged by Brazilians'

wars.outcome: Independentist victory: Salvador surrendered on 2 July 1823, Cochrane secured Maranhão and Pará, the Royal Volunteers left Cisplatina at the beginning of 1824; the Treaty of Rio de Janeiro (29 August 1825, in force 15 November 1825) ended the war.
wars.note: The page dates the war's formal start 1 August 1822 (infobox 1 August 1822 - 29 August 1825) and gives no year for the northern surrender; the John Pascoe Grenfell page puts the Belém mission in August 1823 and the capitulation before 17 October 1823.

wars.name: Confederation of the Equator

zones.text: Olinda, which Paes de Andrade held in 1824

wars.outcome: Proclaimed on 2 July 1824; Olinda and a few villages of southern Ceará and Paraíba; the army attacked Recife on 12 September and the rebels were defeated five days later. Frei Caneca was executed on 13 January 1825.

wars.name: Cisplatine War

zones.text: Cisplatina, where the Portuguese regiments 'retreated to Montevideo and were besieged by Brazilians'

wars.outcome: Brazil declared war on 10 December 1825 (infobox 10 December 1825 - 27 August 1828); there was fighting at Sarandí (12 October 1825) and Ituzaingó/Passo do Rosário (20 February 1827), the Argentines defeated the Brazilian flotilla at Juncal, and Brazil blockaded Buenos Aires; the 1828 convention made Cisplatina independent as Uruguay.

wars.name: Cabanagem

zones.text: the province of Grão-Pará: Belém and the interior where the rebels resisted

wars.outcome: The rebels took Belém on 6 January 1835, left it in April 1836 and resisted in the interior until the last group yielded in 1840; more than 40,000 dead.

wars.name: Ragamuffin War

zones.text: Santa Catarina, where the rebels took Laguna in 1839

wars.outcome: The Riograndense Republic was proclaimed on 11 September 1836; the Juliana Republic of 1839 lasted four months; the Treaty of Ponche Verde of 1 March 1845 reintegrated both.

wars.name: Paraguayan War

zones.text: the southern Mato Grosso districts Paraguay overran (same zone as the paraguay dossier)
São Borja, Itaqui and Uruguaiana (same zone as the paraguay dossier)
the Paraguayan land the Allies overran in 1868-1870, as Cliopatria's Brazil shape draws it

wars.outcome: Paraguay invaded Mato Grosso (14 December 1864) and Rio Grande do Sul (June 1865); the Allies invaded Paraguay on 16 April 1866, took Humaitá on 25 July 1868 and Asunción on 1 January 1869; López died at Cerro Corá on 1 March 1870; the Loizaga-Cotegipe Treaty (9 January 1872) left Brazil the northern regions; the occupation lasted to 1876.
wars.note: The Triple Alliance was Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay (treaty of 1 May 1865); Argentina's dossier slug in Cliopatria is argentine-confederation to 1929.

certainty.note: No treaty fixes the Amazon, Mato Grosso or Missions frontiers; the Cisplatina limit is a war line to 1828.

Treaty lines exist with Uruguay (1851), Peru (1851 and 1874), Bolivia (27 March 1867) and Paraguay (9 January 1872), but 'demarcation of the borders was not started until the end of the 19th century' and the Amazon frontier is approximate; the Uruguay and Paraguay lines are sharp in law.

notes: Cliopatria's 1822 outline is the claimed extent: Portuguese garrisons held Salvador, São Luís, Belém and Montevideo, so the ledger draws four contests with the Portuguese Empire to 1823-1824; the Portuguese Empire row has no Brazilian land after 1821. Maranhão and Pará fell in 1823 (Grenfell page: mission to Belém in August 1823, capitulation before 17 October; Cochrane page: Maranhão undated, after 21 March 1823), confidence 2. Occupation, both ways: the Paraguayan hold on southern Mato Grosso (14 December 1864 to 1868) and on São Borja-Uruguaiana (12 June to 18 September 1865) is recorded as occupation_start/occupation_end with the paraguay dossier's regions (they were contest events in the first draft; the owner mirrors paraguay /ledger/4, 6, 7, 10), and the 1865 outline gets the occupied cells back (status adjust). The end of the Mato Grosso hold is 1868 at confidence 2 (Mato Grosso campaign infobox: 'Paraguayan withdrawal in 1868'; the Paraguayan War page's 'The Brazilians withdrew from the area in April 1868' is about Brazilian troops). The 1868 and 1870 outlines include 534 and 697 cells of Paraguay that are the Allied occupation (1868-1876), removed in the verdicts and carried by an occupation event. North of the Apa: the 345-cell strip (87,250 km2, Paraguay's 1822 shape inside Brazil) is in Cliopatria's Brazil shape from 1868, but the pages date its transfer to the Loizaga-Cotegipe Treaty of 9 January 1872 and no page describes a Brazilian occupation of it in 1868-1871; the 1868 and 1870 corrections subtract it and the 1872 gain mirrors the paraguay dossier's loss. DISAGREEMENT TO RESOLVE in the paraguay dossier (am-08-a): its 1868 and 1870 corrections (intersect with modern Paraguay) drop the strip four years early too, so it is nobody's in 1868-1871 until paraguay keeps it to 1872; its 1866 correction also adds the occupied Mato Grosso land to Paraguay's own outline, whereas occupied land stays the owner's (rule 4). Treaty of Ayacucho: all the Brazilian gains of 1868 outside the strip come from Bolivia's 1866 shape (907 cells): 646 in Amazonas, Rondônia and Acre (about 163,000 km2) at confidence 2, and 261 in western Mato Grosso, Mato Grosso do Sul and Santa Cruz (about 65,000 km2) at confidence 1; the page names only 102,400 km2 and no line. Not settled: the 1853 jump of 200,803 km2 in the north-west Amazon (confidence 1, from nobody; the Venezuela 1859, Colombia 1907/1928 and Peru 1909 pages put the treaty lines later and describe no 1853 transfer; the 1851 Peru treaty is not on any page opened), the 1877 +40 cells of Roraima (a confidence 1 gain from nobody; the Brazil-Venezuela page is silent), the 13 Amazonas cells of 1825. Not added: the Allied invasion of Paraguay as a contest mirror of paraguay /ledger/9 and 12 (1866-04 to 1870-03; wars[5] carries the zone and /ledger occupation 1868-07 follows it). The Cabanagem rebels (Pará, 6 January 1835 to 1840) and the Confederation of the Equator (2 July - September 1824) are counterparts without a Cliopatria row or a dossier; neither page opened mentions a proclamation of independence for Pará, so they are left as named counterparts. Slivers of Argentina (Misiones, Corrientes), Uruguay and Bolivia (Santa Cruz 36 cells, El Beni 22) sit inside the outline in 1885 and are not explained by any page. The infobox area 8,337,218 km2 is for 1889; the 1885-1889 shape is 8,356,869 km2 (ratio 1.002).
